1:
Why Judah drew first is answered at three depths. Henry begins from the birthright: Judah and Joseph were the two sons of Jacob on whom Reuben's forfeiture devolved, the dominion entailed on the one and the double portion on the other, so these two were seated before the rest — Judah in the south, Joseph in the north — with the other seven attending on them, Benjamin, Simeon and Dan appendant to Judah, the remaining four to Joseph. Ellicott looks further back and finds a cause in two earlier promises: Hebron had been promised to Caleb and Shechem assigned to Joseph by Jacob, and he asks whether that did not of itself bring Judah into the south and Ephraim into the centre. Calvin reads the same fact as prophecy discharging itself. The names went into the urn and Judah came out first, raised to the highest rank so that Jacob's word might be fulfilled; the territory itself lies high, its very elevation a presage of the coming kingdom's dignity, and within those limits were rich pastures and vineyards famous for their wines. Nothing here happened by chance — the patriarch had only uttered what the Spirit dictated three centuries before.

How the lot was actually cast interests Wesley most. It was transacted with great solemnity in God's presence, with prayer and appeal to him for the decision; and since no exact survey existed yet, there must have been a general description of the land and a division into nine parts and a half, made as nearly equal in quantity or quality as could be guessed. He supposes two pots, one holding the names of the tribes and the other the names of the portions, a name drawn from each in turn — which is why the lots are spoken of as coming up or coming forth, the papers lying in the bottom. Gill sets the two occasions apart: the first casting, for Judah and Joseph, was at Gilgal, and only afterwards were lots cast at Shiloh for the seven tribes lying between them.

How far down the lot reached is disputed. Gill takes it to have governed the subdivision as well, each tribe's portion being distributed by lot among its families and households. Clarke denies it: the family divisions were left to Joshua, Eleazar and the ten princes, who appointed each family a district in proportion to its numbers, the general division alone being determined by lot. Wesley agrees that the lot settled only which part belonged to each tribe and left the particulars to Joshua and Eleazar, and adds that it did not settle even that unchangeably, since Simeon's portion was afterwards taken out of Judah's.

Clarke meets the difficulty a chapter of place-names raises before he begins. Many of these towns have had their names so wholly changed that the old ones are no longer discernible, and some lie buried under their own ruins — which embarrasses a commentator without touching the truth of the narrative. He presses the point by comparison: where now are Babylon, Nineveh, Carthage, Thebes, Tyre, Baalbec, Palmyra, or the greatly celebrated Troy? Scarcely a vestige of any remains, and the learned cannot agree on the ground they stood on; if that does not invalidate the history of the ancient world, neither does it here. Enough of these places survive, under their old names or with characteristics decisive enough that the ancient name shows through the new. On why Joshua is so particular about this tribe's limits Clarke follows Calmet: it was the first, the most numerous and the most important, it was to furnish the kings of Judea, pure religion was to be preserved in it, and the Messiah was to spring from it. Keil and Delitzsch note the providence in the placing: the inheritance fell in the south where Caleb had his, so that he was not separated from his own tribe.
2:
The sea the line starts from is described before the line is traced. Gill gives its several names — the dead sea, the sea of Sodom, the lake Asphaltites — and places it, with Jarchi, to the south-east of the land. Wesley renders the bay by its Hebrew word, a tongue, meaning either a creek or arm of the water or else a promontory, which learned writers sometimes call by that name; and he accounts for the epithet by the catastrophe. Every sea is salt, but this one has an extraordinary saltness, the effect of the fire and brimstone that destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, whose ruins lie buried at the bottom of a dead water which no tide ever moved and in which nothing ever lived. Keil and Delitzsch are drier about it: the line began from the southern point of the sea, now a salt marsh, and this was the southern boundary not of Judah only but of the whole land, coinciding with the border Moses had already laid down.

The stations along it are identified with varying confidence. Keil and Delitzsch make the ascent of Akrabbim the row of lofty whitish cliffs that cuts across the Arabah some eight miles below the Dead Sea, Zin the Wady Murreh, and Kadesh-barnea the spring called Ain Kudes. Clarke reads Akrabbim as the ascent of the Mount of Scorpions, probably named from the multitude of those animals found there, and fills in Kadesh-barnea's history: it had been called Enmishpat, lay on the edge of the wilderness of Paran some twenty-four miles from Hebron, and was where Miriam died and where Moses and Aaron rebelled, so that it took the further name of the contention of Kadesh. For Karkaa he follows Calmet, who takes it for the Coracea of Ptolemy in Arabia Petraea. Ellicott quotes Conder's survey for the shape of the whole: the border runs east to west and afterwards became Simeon's, and though not every point is certainly known, the great mountain wall reaching from the Dead Sea to the watershed south of Rehoboth was the natural and recognised boundary of Palestine. Conder also offers a fresh identification for Hezron, the point next to Kadesh-barnea on the west — a mountain called Hadireh lying immediately west of the valley in which Kadesh probably stood, the name being radically the same.

Over the river of Egypt the readings part. Clarke first calls it the most eastern branch of the Nile, then withdraws his confidence: there is much reason to doubt whether any branch of the Nile is meant, or whether the promised land reached that river at all, and he thinks it impossible to decide either way. Conder, quoted by Ellicott, has no such hesitation and takes it for the present Wady el-Arish, the northern boundary between Syria and Egypt; Keil and Delitzsch agree, tracing the wady as it turns north and then north-west to open into the Mediterranean. Gill and Clarke agree at least about Azmon, the last town held on that side, which Jerome knew as Asemona, a city in the desert dividing Egypt from Judah's lot.

One phrase in the middle of all this catches Ellicott's ear. This shall be your south coast does not match the language around it, and he reads it as a reminiscence of Moses: the whole passage runs very close to the earlier description of the land's borders, but where Moses wrote in the second person and the future tense throughout, Joshua writes in the third person and the past — except just here, where he seems to have slipped unconsciously into the phrasing of the lawgiver rather than the historian.
5:
Of the eastern line there is little to say beyond its length, and Gill measures it from the ancients: five hundred and eighty furlongs by Josephus, a hundred miles by Pliny. Clarke simply runs it down the whole length of the Dead Sea, from the sea's lowest extremity to the place where Jordan falls into it.

The northern line is another matter, and it is traced with unusual precision because it doubles as Benjamin's southern one. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the same border is described again later in the opposite direction, from west to east, and they fix its early stations closely. Beth-hoglah they identify with Ain Hajla, an hour and a quarter south-east of Jericho and three-quarters of an hour from the river; Gill reaches nearly the same spot by another road, citing Jerome for a place called Betagla three miles from Jericho and two from Jordan. Beth-arabah, a town of the desert of Judah later assigned to Benjamin, Keil and Delitzsch put twenty or thirty minutes south-west of the first, in a level and barren steppe with which its name agrees well. They also note that the verb is went up, which registers the climb out of the valley.

Two of the markers resist identification altogether. Clarke takes the stone of Bohan for some notable spot, like the stone of Jacob that afterwards became Bethel, but will not say where it stood; Wesley adds that it cannot be named from Bohan's dwelling there, since the Reubenites had no portion on this side of Jordan, and supposes instead some exploit of his that Scripture does not record. The Debir named here is not the town of that name in Gad, Gill insists, nor the one near Hebron, but a third lying not far from Jericho; Keil and Delitzsch would look for it by the Wady Daber, which runs down to the Dead Sea, perhaps near the rocky grotto called Choret ed Daber on the road between Jerusalem and Jericho; Clarke calls it simply unknown. The Gilgal the line turns north toward is not, on Keil's reading, the camp of the crossing, which he is careful not to confound with it.

Ellicott follows Conder over the same ground with a surveyor's map in hand, and the modern names come with reasons attached. The border started at the Jordan mouth but did not follow the river, since Beth-arabah and Beth-hoglah belonged to Benjamin; it passed along the valley of Achor — which keeps the memory of Achan's punishment, as Clarke notes — left Gilgal to the north, and climbed the pass to the going up of Adummim, now Tal'at-ed-Dumm. Both the ancient name and the modern one mean bloody, which Conder derives from the brick-red marls lying there in a district of white chalk, though Ellicott remarks drily that other reasons are easy to conjecture. A line of Roman road on the survey he offers as a fair guide to the boundary along this stretch. En-shemesh, the fountain of the sun, lay east of Jerusalem on the line between the two tribes, and En-rogel, the next known point, close by Zoheleth, Conder takes for the spring now called Ain Umm-ed-Deraj in the Kedron valley.
8:
The valley the border climbs through is the one place here every commentator wants to talk about, and they cannot agree where it lay. Gill reports Jerome putting it east of Jerusalem while Reland prefers the south; Clarke places it east without qualification; Keil and Delitzsch put it south of Mount Zion. Who Hinnom was neither Clarke nor Keil can say; nothing is known of him but that he owned it. What they do agree on is what happened there. The image of Moloch stood in it and children were made to pass through the fire, a worship Keil dates as notorious from the time of Ahaz, and Clarke adds what became of the place after Josiah removed the idol: it was held in such execration that it turned into the general receptacle for the filth carried out of Jerusalem, with fires kept burning to consume the refuse and prevent infection. From the Hebrew for the valley of the son of Hinnom, contracted, came the Gehenna of the New Testament, the emblem of hell.

Two smaller observations attach here. Clarke notices the idiom that names a son by his father and remarks that in the East the addition is not made until the father's death, a custom he says prevailed in the west too and is common still among the aborigines of Ireland and Wales. Gill and Wesley both stop on the verb: the border is repeatedly said to go up because the ground climbs from Jordan and the salt sea toward Jerusalem, and Wesley notes that the same line goes down where a later chapter traces it the contrary way.

The city itself raises a harder question, since the line runs along its edge. Clarke observes that it was formerly Jebus, that part of it lay in Benjamin, and that Zion, its citadel, was Judah's. Wesley grants that Jerusalem looks principally Benjamin's and offers two ways it might be ascribed to Judah: either part of the city was allotted to Judah outright, or the Benjamites wanted the help of so powerful a neighbour in taking and holding a place of that importance — and since Benjamin tried in vain to expel the Jebusites and Judah at length did it, Judah had an interest by right of war, as Ziklag belonged to Simeon until David, taking it from the Philistines, joined it to his tribe.

Clarke prints a note from a clerical correspondent working the same ground more finely. The boundary went up from Hinnom eastward to the hilltop southward, leaving Jebus to the north-west against Benjamin, so that the mount lay between the tribes and stayed Jebusite until David; Zion and Moriah, where the temple stood, were Judah's. He reads the blessing that has the Lord dwelling by Benjamin, between his shoulders, as suggesting a line curving so as partly to encompass Mount Zion, and explains Benjamin's gate and the gate of Ephraim as leading out toward those tribes, much as roads are named now. Calvary he places in Benjamin, and closes with a query: was Golgotha so called from skulls scattered about, as some say, or from the rock being shaped like a skull with one face nearly perpendicular? He inclines to the second, believing the Jews would not have suffered human bones, even a malefactor's, to lie about.

After the city the line runs to quieter places. Keil and Delitzsch identify the fountain of the waters of Nephtoah with the village of Liftah an hour north-west of Jerusalem, where a copious spring bearing Samuel's name fills large basins and waters blooming gardens, and take the towns of Mount Ephron for the steep ridge west of the terebinth valley. Baalah, the text says, is Kirjath-jearim; Conder, quoted by Ellicott, identifies it with 'Arma, four miles east of Beth-shemesh, and Clarke recalls why the name is remembered: the ark rested there twenty years after the Philistines sent it back.
10:
The mountain the border turns to has a famous name and no settled place. Gill insists it is not the Seir of Idumea, so notorious as the seat of Esau and lying far from here, but a third of that name near Kirjath-jearim, which Adrichomius sets on the borders of Azotus and Ashkelon; Wesley supposes it was called so from some resemblance to the other; Ellicott agrees that it is entirely distinct from the place in Edom and adds that it has not been precisely identified. Keil and Delitzsch are willing to name it — the ridge of rock south-west of Kureyet el Enab, a lofty range of rugged peaks with a wild and desolate look about it.

The next stations they and Conder identify alike. Chesalon is the present Kesla, on the summit of a mountain in the high ridge between two wadys, which Conder fixes at two and a quarter miles due north of Khurbet 'Erma; Timnah, on the same survey, is Tibneh. Beth-shemesh Keil and Delitzsch note as a priests' city, the same place as Ir-shemesh on the border of Dan, where the Philistines set down the ark. Clarke takes the name apart instead — the house or temple of the sun — and reads it as evidence that the sun was an object of adoration among the Canaanites, who dedicated fountains and hills to him; and he recalls the town's other distinction, the slaughter of its people for prying curiously, if not impiously, into the ark when it was sent back.

At Ekron the line reaches Philistine country, and Ellicott marks the change of terrain: this is the Shephelah, the plain of the sea-coast. Gill notes the awkwardness of the arrangement — Ekron was one of the principalities of the Philistines, and though it fell within Judah's lot, Judah never possessed it. Keil and Delitzsch trace the last stretch with a caution against over-confidence. Shichron may be Sugheir, an hour south-west of Jebna, on Knobel's suggestion; but if so, they argue, the mountain of Baalah cannot be the low range west of Akir that Knobel proposes, since the boundary has already crossed the intervening wady, and it must instead be a mountain on the southern side. Jabneel they identify securely as the Philistine Jabneh whose walls Uzziah broke down, the Jamnia of Josephus and the books of Maccabees, still standing as a good-sized village called Jebnah; Conder places it west of Ekron, nearer the sea.

The western border needs no tracing at all. Gill and Clarke dispose of it in a line: the great sea is the Mediterranean, and Judah's coast ran along it from Jabneel down to the river of Egypt, where the southern border had ended — which closes the circuit begun at the salt sea and completes the boundary of the tribe according to its families.
13:
Gill explains why the grant is repeated here: it stands before the list of Judah's cities to show what had to be excepted from them, Caleb's portion having been settled before the lot was cast. Keil and Delitzsch read the verb as impersonal — they gave, meaning Joshua gave — and refer the clause about the commandment of the Lord back to the promise made in Joshua's own hearing at Kadesh. Wesley corrects the scope: what Caleb received was not the city of Arba, which fell to the Levites, but its territory.

Henry finds the historian pleased with every occasion of doing Caleb honour, because Caleb had honoured God by following him fully, and notices two things in the grant. Caleb had a good title by promise; but since God had ordered the land divided by lot, Joshua would not depart from that even to gratify an old friend without consulting the oracle first — in every doubtful case, Henry adds, it is desirable to know the mind of God and see one's duty plain. And though the portion was assigned before Judah's lot came up, God so directed the lot that it fell in the heart of that tribe, so that Caleb was not left separated from his brethren and surrounded by strangers.

Calvin puts the same grant under a harder light. Judging by the state of things at the time, it would look ridiculous to keep celebrating a grant from which Caleb drew no benefit while Joshua lived; sneering men, and the inhabitants of the place if word had reached them, might have laughed at Caleb's vain solicitude and Joshua's empty liberality. The mockery would only have proved them scoffers. God showed the firmness of his decree by the outcome at last, and Caleb, seeing that he could not so much as get access to the mountain, was content with the bare promise — which Calvin makes the definition of the thing: faith is exercised precisely in a willingness to go without what has been promised until the time for it arrives. He adds that the giants of that country were named from their progenitor, so that the word is of Gentile origin, and that Caleb's appeal to Moses was no pretence, since the text plainly declares Moses had so appointed at God's command.

How the giants went is a point Henry will not let pass. The text says Caleb drove them thence, not that he slew them, which he takes to mean they retired at his approach and fled — the strength of their bodies could not keep up the courage of their minds, and with the countenances of lions they had the hearts of trembling hares. So, on his reading, God cuts off the spirit of princes and shames the confidence of the proud; and so the devil, that roaring lion, will flee when resisted even if he does not fall.

Henry also looks ahead to the second campaign and makes much of it. Joshua had once mastered Debir and the Canaanites had regained it in the army's absence, so the work had to be done over; and Caleb, with his own portion already secure, pushed on ten miles to a town in which he had no private interest at all. That, for Henry, is zeal for the common good rather than for his own, and the lesson he draws is that we are not born for ourselves and must not mind our own things only. The town's older name puzzles him as it puzzles everyone else: some translate its variant form as the city of letters, from which he conjectures either a Canaanite university, an Athens of that country, or a repository where the chronicles of the nation were laid up — and perhaps that is what made Caleb want it, so that Israel might come at the ancient learning of the Canaanites.
14:
When the expulsion happened is disputed, and so is who performed it. Gill reports the view that it fell after Joshua's death and was inserted here by another inspired hand, so that the gift and the possession might appear together, but himself thinks it was done earlier. Calvin holds the opposite: it plainly took place afterwards, and the writer set it down here so that no ambiguity should remain about Judah's lot — and about the still odder business of a fertile, well-watered field passing to a woman. Keil and Delitzsch face the other difficulty, that Judges credits the sons of Judah generally with driving out the Anakites. The one does not preclude the other, since Caleb acted not as an individual but as the head of a Judaean family and with their help. Nor, against Knobel, is there any discrepancy with the earlier record of Joshua taking Hebron and Debir and forcing the Anakites back into the Philistine towns, since being driven out once did not prevent their returning.

Wesley supposes exactly that: the giants had either recovered their cities or held out in caves and forts among the mountains, and what Caleb drove them from was the territory. Whether the three men named were the ones the spies had seen he leaves open — either they were long-lived, as men commonly were in those times and places, or these were their sons bearing their fathers' names, which he notes is usual enough.

The town Caleb went on to has two names and neither is transparent. Clarke renders the older one the city of the book and admits that why it was so called is uncertain, noting a third form of the name further down the chapter. Wesley thinks the clause identifying the two names was added precisely to distinguish this Debir from the other town Joshua had subdued. Keil and Delitzsch, who cannot locate it at all, place it south of Hebron and infer from the size of the prize offered that it must have been very strong and hard to take.

Why Caleb offered a prize rather than simply ordering the assault is answered several ways. Gill will not have it that the proclamation betrayed any difficulty beyond the ordinary, or any diffidence in Caleb: the officers and men of valour under him should have a chance to gather laurels as well as their commander, and chiefly Caleb was under a divine impulse, so that his kinsman Othniel — who was to be a judge in Israel — might show himself a great man and fit for the office. Wesley says the same thing about the outcome, that the point was to make Othniel's valour manifest and prepare the way for his future government of the people. Keil and Delitzsch set the offer beside Saul's later promise of his daughter to the conqueror of Goliath, and Clarke generalises it: in ancient times fathers assumed an absolute right over their children in the matter of marriage, and a king or great man promising his daughter to whoever should take a city or kill an enemy was common enough, with many similar examples among profane writers. Wesley qualifies the promise before it can be read as coercion. It must be understood with conditions — that the man be one she could lawfully marry, and that she be willing; for however great the power of parents over children, they could not force them to marry against their own wills.
17:
The kinship is the first thing that has to be sorted out, because as it stands it looks unlawful. Gill lays out the problem: at first sight Othniel is Caleb's own younger brother, and so uncle to the bride, a marriage the law forbade. He canvasses the rabbis — Jarchi makes him a brother by the mother's side only, Kimchi by both parents — and then cuts the knot grammatically. Besides that the word for brother sometimes means no more than a near kinsman, it is not Othniel who is called Caleb's brother in the verse but Kenaz, Othniel's father; so Caleb was Othniel's uncle, and Achsah and Othniel were first cousins, between whom marriage was allowed. Keil and Delitzsch consider the same two readings of the Hebrew and come down the other way. Both are admissible, but the first is the more usual, the received accentuation separates the two phrases in its favour, and it is right, since son of Kenaz is equivalent to the Kenizzite; Othniel was Caleb's younger brother, and marriage with a brother's daughter was not forbidden in the law at all.

What Achsah asked for, and how, is described with unusual attention to gesture. Keil and Delitzsch take the field she wanted to be neither the land belonging to Debir, which went with the town and needed no asking, nor any field at all, but arable ground with springs on it; and they note that the text records only what she did, not what her husband did, possibly because he could not bring himself to put the request. She sprang from the ass she had been riding. Clarke has her alight hastily and suddenly, as though she had forgotten something or were about to turn back to her father's house, which is what prompted him to ask what the matter was; Wesley reads the same movement as deliberate humility, a woman placing herself before her father in the posture of a suppliant, and says he understood her by the gesture.

Calvin gives the episode a severe reading that nothing else here matches. Achsah may be presumed to have been of excellent morals and well brought up, since marriage with her was held out as the special reward of a victory; yet what is disclosed in this scene, he says, is perverse cupidity. She knew that the divine law specially excluded women from hereditary lands, and coveted them anyway, stirring up her husband by an unjust expostulation — and so, he warns, ambitious and covetous wives never cease molesting their husbands until they have made them forget shame and equity. Men's avarice is insatiable too, he grants, but women are apt to be the more precipitate, and husbands should be the more on guard against being blown into flame by such counsels. Her boldness then grows on her husband's compliance and her father's indulgence: not content with a field, she asks a well-watered district, and once a person has overleaped the bounds of rectitude the fault is followed up by impudence. Caleb's refusing her nothing proves his singular affection, but does not make the thirst of gain less hateful. On her dismounting Calvin declines the harsher construction some interpreters put on it — dissimulation, a feigned inability to keep her seat for grief — and prefers the simpler one, that she put herself at her father's feet as a suppliant; though he still holds that by craft and flattery she got his consent and so far reduced her brothers' portions. A note appended to his own text answers him: the censure is more severe than the circumstances warrant, since the preference given to males in succession is only conventional, and by natural law her brothers' title was no better than hers.
19:
What she actually said turns on one word. Gill runs through the possibilities and rejects most of them. She was not asking a paternal benediction, nor that her father would wish and pray a blessing on her, nor food and maintenance — Jarchi's reading, that her husband should provide for her. What she meant was an inheritance or possession, as the Targum has it, or a present over and above what had already been given her, as Abendana takes it, or an addition to her portion, as Kimchi reads it. Gill then notes the point on which the whole request turns: the same word can mean a fish pool as well as a blessing, so that in asking for one she was already glancing at the other, and the petition that follows only makes explicit what the choice of word had implied. Clarke reads it simply as asking a favour, an act of kindness or a particular request; Wesley as asking a gift, in the sense the word carries elsewhere in Scripture. The south land she complains of was dry or ill watered, and Wesley accounts for its condition by its exposure to a south wind that came hot and drying off the deserts of Arabia. What she wanted in exchange Clarke describes concretely: fields with brooks or wells already dug in them. Wesley adds why such a thing was worth asking for — springs were of great price in that country — and reads her petition as covering both needs at once, a well-moistened field that might also give some relief to the barren ground she already held.

Her father gave her more than she asked. Clarke has him grant a district among the mountains and another in the plains, both well situated and well watered, and closes by admitting that several difficulties attend the account which he will not trouble the reader with, the sense given being the best he can make of it. Wesley takes the upper and nether springs for two fields lying above and below the parched ground, so that it might be watered from both sides. With that the account of Caleb's portion is done, and Keil and Delitzsch mark the next verse as the formula which rounds off the description of Judah's territory by its boundaries before the list of its towns begins.
20:
Gill marks the join: the general description is done and the particular cities follow, the business of Hebron and Debir having stood between as a parenthesis. Henry says why the towns are named at all — so that the people might know their own, keep it and keep to it, and lose nothing through cowardice or sloth. Keil and Delitzsch supply the plan: four districts answering to the nature of the ground — the south land, the lowland toward the Mediterranean, the mountains, and the desert of Judah — the first running in its full extent from the Arabah at the south end of the Dead Sea across to the coast.

The arithmetic does not work, and three ways of mending it are on offer. Henry counts thirty-eight names in this first district against a total of twenty-nine, and accounts for the gap by the nine towns afterwards transferred to Simeon, so that only what remained to Judah was counted. Wesley allows that and offers another beside it: perhaps only twenty-nine were cities properly so called, that is walled, or having villages under them, the rest being large but unwalled towns. Clarke suspects the trouble is textual — several places here are named by compound terms, and translators unfamiliar with them have combined or divided the words wrongly. The same difficulty recurs in the next district, where fifteen names are counted as fourteen; Henry supposes two of them to be two parts of one town.

Calvin is interested in the total rather than the discrepancy, and makes it a hundred and thirteen cities with their towns and villages, where Henry's reckoning of the whole comes to a hundred and fourteen. The number, on his reading, attests the populousness of the country and its fertility together — a fertility he takes to have been increased by the divine blessing, though God's goodness appeared already in the choice of a land abounding in every advantage. Set the number of souls in the tribe against the space, he says, and half of it would have amply sufficed: allow eight hundred to a city and the rest still had the towns and villages to live in. That is why a portion could afterwards be withdrawn for Simeon, and in that withdrawal he sees Jacob's word about dispersion carried out, the Simeonites being admitted by Judah as a kind of guests.

One absence strikes Henry more than any of the names present. Bethlehem is not in the list — the town afterwards made David's city and ennobled by the birth of Christ, which at its best was little among the thousands of Judah and was then not accounted a city at all, but one of the unnamed villages. He makes the omission a principle: Christ came to give honour to the places he was related to, not to take honour from them.

The rest of the names Henry reads forward into the history they were going to have. Libnah revolted in Joram's days and probably set up as a free state; Lachish, where Amaziah was slain, led the dance in idolatry and was the beginning of sin to the daughter of Zion; Giloh was Ahithophel's town; Tekoa produced Amos; at Maresha Asa was conqueror. A cluster of them belongs to David's wanderings — Adullam, Ziph, Keilah, Maon, Engedi, Ziklag — for though Saul drove him from the inheritance of the Lord he kept as close to it as he could; and the wilderness of Judah, which he frequented, was where John afterwards preached. Clarke annotates several of the same places: Ziph sheltered David and its inhabitants then tried to hand him over; Beer-sheba was the residence of Abraham and of Jacob, forty miles from Jerusalem on the road to Egypt; Hormah was made famous by a defeat of the Hebrews; and Ziklag stayed in Philistine hands until Achish gave it to David.
33:
Keil and Delitzsch describe the country before listing what stood in it. The lowland is the land between the mountains of Judah and the Mediterranean, a broad plain of undulating appearance cut by heights and low ranges of hills, with soil fertile enough that cornfields alternate with meadows, gardens and extensive olive groves; the Greek translators usually rendered the word simply as the plain, but in the prophets carried it over untranslated as a proper name. Ellicott gives the same identification in a phrase — the plain of the coast — and then does something the older commentators do not, which is to count how much is recoverable: of the fourteen towns in the first group Conder identifies ten, and of the sixteen in the second, seven. Gill fixes the district by Jerome, who reports that in his day the whole plain and champaign country about Eleutheropolis, running north and west, was still called by the old name.

Two of the first names have a history outside this chapter. Clarke notes that Samson was buried at Zoreah, it being the burial place of his fathers, and that these towns, though given here to Judah, afterwards fell to the lot of Dan; Ellicott records the same transfer. Of Socoh, Clarke remarks that it was near this place that David fought and killed the Philistine champion. Keil and Delitzsch supply its later fortunes and its site: Rehoboam fortified it, the Philistines took it in the reign of Ahaz, and it survives as Shuweikeh by the Wady Sumt, half an hour south-west of Jarmuth — though they note that the Onomasticon knew two villages of the name, one on the mountain and one in the plain, nine Roman miles from Eleutheropolis on the road to Jerusalem.

Where identification rests on argument rather than survival, Keil and Delitzsch show their working. Sharaim they place at Tell Zakariya and the village facing it across a deep valley only twenty minutes broad, and the reason they give is grammatical: the Hebrew name is a dual, and the site comes in two halves. Gill reaches for Jerome again here, and for a village on the borders of Eleutheropolis about ten miles out on the Nicopolis road. Gederah they take, more tentatively, for the Gederoth the Philistines seized under Ahaz. They are equally willing to say when an identification fails. Knobel's proposal for Dilean they reject on the plain ground that the ruins he points to lie upon the mountains and not in the plain, which is where the text puts the town. Mizpeh, whose name means a watchtower, they distinguish from the Mizpeh of Benjamin and place north of Eleutheropolis on the authority of the Onomasticon, suggesting the medieval castle called Alba Specula, now Tell es Saphieh, standing on a lofty hill in the middle of the plain with a prospect in every direction — a site that would earn the name.

The rest are a mixture of the settled and the lost. Lachish and Eglon they identify with Um Lakis and Ajlan, and Clarke refers both back to the earlier campaign in which they fell. Bozkath is unknown, though Knobel would put it at some ruins to the south. Cabbon is probably the heap of ruins called Kubeibeh, which must once have been a strong fortification and, on Van de Velde's judgment, formed the key to the central mountains of Judah. Beth-dagon defeats them. Clarke reads the name as the house or temple of Dagon, a well-known idol of the Philistines, and infers that the place lay somewhere in their territory, but says its situation is now unknown; Keil and Delitzsch add the negative result of the obvious guess, since the village the Onomasticon calls by that name, between Diospolis and Jamnia, lies far beyond Judah's northern boundary and cannot be it.
42:
Keil and Delitzsch open the third group: the towns of the southern half of the hilly region, nine of them. Gill marks the same break at Libnah, which he identifies with the royal city taken earlier in the book. From there the ground goes soft. Ether and Ashan were afterwards given to the Simeonites, as Clarke notes, and are probably to be looked for on the border of the south country; neither has been found, and the guess that connects Ether with some ruins in the province of Gaza Keil and Delitzsch call very uncertain. Ashan they take, more confidently, for the place that appears under a longer name in David's history and became a priests' city later. Jiphtah, Ashnah and Nezib they have not traced at all. Ellicott, counting again, reports that Conder identifies five of the nine.

Keilah is the one place in the group with a history, and the commentators divide over where it stood. Clarke puts it near Hebron and adds the tradition that Habakkuk was buried there, together with the episode that made the town memorable: David forced the Philistines to raise their siege of it, then learned that the men he had saved meant to hand him over to Saul, and got away. Gill locates it by Jerome, a little village eight miles east of Eleutheropolis on the road to Hebron, where the prophet's sepulchre was shown. Keil and Delitzsch reject both that site and Knobel's alternative, and on the same principle in each case: the traditional village lies upon the mountains of Judah and Knobel's ruins south of the mountains of Hebron, whereas a town in this list must be sought in the lowland, or at the least to the west or south-west of those mountains. Achzib they identify with an earlier Chesib and place at some ruins with a fountain. Mareshah Clarke fills out from later history — the birthplace of Micah, and the field of the great battle in which Asa met a host of a thousand thousand men and three hundred chariots, defeated it, and took much spoil.

The fourth group is of a different character altogether, being the Philistine line of coast. Gill states the awkward fact plainly: Ekron was one of the five principalities, and it and the two towns named after it fell within Judah's lot and were never possessed. He suggests that is why Gath and Ashkelon go unmentioned, these three standing for the rest. Keil and Delitzsch account for the same silence better: both are included inside the boundaries actually named, Ashkelon lying between Ashdod and Gaza on the coast and Gath east of Ekron and Ashdod, so that each fell to Judah as a matter of course. They give the same reason for the thinness of the intervening verse — the places between Ekron and the sea are not listed because Judah never came into possession of them. Ellicott notes that Ekron itself was afterwards assigned to Dan, and Keil and Delitzsch that the northern part of this coastal strip went the same way while remaining almost entirely in Philistine hands.

Against the critics who would strike these verses out as spurious or a later interpolation, Keil and Delitzsch make a short answer. The arguments rest on two assertions — that the writer names only towns the Hebrews held in his own day, and that his lowland list never approaches the sea — and neither, they say, has anything to support it. Of the towns themselves little is left to add. Ashdod and Gaza they identify by the modern names of both sites; Clarke notes that Ashdod appears in the New Testament as Azotus, takes the great sea for the Mediterranean, and reverts to his earlier hesitation over the river of Egypt, naming the Pelusiac branch of the Nile while referring the reader back to the doubt he had already entered.
48:
Wesley marks the change of district in the simplest possible terms: the mountains are the higher ground, so called by comparison with the sea-coast just left behind. Keil and Delitzsch describe what that ground is. The mountains of Judah rise sharply out of the south country, between the hilly belt on the west that counts as part of the lowland and the desert running down to the Dead Sea on the east; near Hebron they reach three thousand feet above the sea, and they run north to the broad wady above Jerusalem — a large rugged range of limestone. The towns on them are divided, they say, into five groups, or more accurately six.

Gill names the district by the phrase later usage settled on, the hill country of Judea. Identification here goes better than it did in the plain, and Ellicott's tally records it: of the nine towns in the second group six have been found. Keil and Delitzsch place Eshtemoh, a town afterwards ceded to the priests, at the inhabited village of Semua east of Socoh, where walls and an ancient castle remain, and derive Anim by contraction from a word meaning fountains, the name surviving in ruins nearby. Anab they set north-east of Socoh. Clarke's notes on this stretch are mostly cross-references, except where a name has a story attached to it: Giloh, he observes, was the country of the traitor Ahithophel.

Two of the names raise questions bigger than their sites. Goshen is one, since some would make it the source of the name in the phrase about the land of Goshen earlier in the book; Ellicott doubts it, on the ground that this place is insignificant and unidentified, and thinks it much more reasonable to take that phrase as meaning frontier or border land. Kirjath-arba is the other, and needs no locating at all — Clarke simply refers the reader back to Hebron, the town this whole chapter began with, which appears here in its list like any other. Ellicott adds Giloh's later fame as the home of Ahithophel the Gilonite, counsellor first to David and then to Absalom.

What these groups have in common is that the country is high, dry and thinly held, and the commentators treat the list accordingly. Where a name occurs only here and nowhere else in Scripture, Gill and Keil alike say so and pass on — Dannah is their standing example; where a modern village or a heap of ruins preserves the sound of the Hebrew, they give the distance and the direction from a known point and leave the reader to judge. Ellicott's practice is to count rather than to argue, so that each group carries its own measure of how much of it can still be found — which is, in a chapter that is otherwise a bare catalogue, the nearest thing to an admission of how much has been lost.
55:
The third group runs east of the other two, toward the desert, and it is the one district in this chapter that later history crowded with incident. Keil and Delitzsch locate Maon, Nabal's home, at Tell Main on a conical hill commanding a wide prospect, some three and three-quarter hours south by east of Hebron, and note that the desert on whose border it stood is called the desert of Maon in David's story. Clarke adds that David took refuge for a considerable time in that desert, and that Carmel here is not the celebrated mountain of the name but the village where Nabal lived, about ten miles east of Hebron. Wesley notes that Ziph likewise gave its name to the mountains around it, and Gill that the wilderness where David hid from Saul took its name from Maon, placing the town by Jerome east of Daroma, where a village of the name still stood in his day.

Ellicott gathers the group's reputation into a sentence and does not soften it. Maon, Carmel and Ziph became famous in David's wanderings, and the Ziphites, he says, covered themselves with infamy by their repeated efforts to betray him to the king who was seeking his life. He also counts, as usual: the four first and the four last of the ten have all been found. Of the remainder Keil and Delitzsch can say only that the Jezreel named here — the home of one of David's wives, and a different place from the Jezreel of the northern plain — has not been discovered, and that two more of the names occur nowhere else at all; Gill says the same, and wonders aloud about Cain, whether the old Canaanites gave the place that name in memory of Adam's son, which he will not determine. Timnah, on the other hand, Clarke identifies as the Philistine frontier town where Samson got his wife.

The next group brings the sharpest textual question in the chapter. Clarke reports that at this point the Alexandrian manuscript of the Septuagint and the Vatican codex insert eleven further towns — among them Ephratha, which is to say Bethlehem — with the closing formula naming them as eleven cities and their villages; and that Jerome mentions them, so they stood in the copies he used. Kennicott argues they should be restored to the text, and explains the loss mechanically: the phrase and their villages occurs immediately before the passage and again at the end of it, so the transcriber's eye jumped from the one to the other, an accident he compares with the omission of two whole verses in a later chapter. Keil and Delitzsch record the same gap, placing the missing group north of the fourth and reaching as far as Jerusalem, in a district where at least fifteen places and ruins can still be counted.

Its bearing is not confined to arithmetic. If the eleven belong to the text, then Bethlehem's absence from Judah's cities — which has been read as a measure of how little the town then was — is a copyist's slip rather than a fact about Bethlehem. Gill opens the fourth group at Halhul, which Jerome knew as a village near Hebron. Of the sixth group Ellicott reports that five of its six towns have been identified, and Keil and Delitzsch that Maarath and Eltekon are not among them, while Beth-anoth — probably a contraction of a longer name — was found by Wolcott in the ruins of Beit-anum. The two towns that close the mountain district give no trouble at all: Kirjath-baal is the Kirjath-jearim already met on the boundary line, and Rabbah is marked on the survey as Rubba.
61:
How bad the country is depends on who is describing it. Keil and Delitzsch call it for the most part a terrible desert — a soil of chalk, marl and limestone, bald mountains covered with flint and hornstone, and on the side bordering the Dead Sea not the slightest trace of vegetation — and they fix its extent, running along that sea from the northern border of the tribe down to a wady in the south and reaching west as far as the districts of Maon, Ziph, Tekoah and Bethlehem. Gill enters a quiet correction before the list begins: the wilderness of Judea was not a desert and uninhabited, but had many cities and villages in it, the ones that follow. That six towns are counted in so bare a tract is itself the notable thing.

Of the six towns, three can be found and three cannot. Ellicott names the three that have been identified — Secacah, the city of Salt, and Engedi — and Keil and Delitzsch confirm that Nibshan is unknown; Gill notes that no mention is made of it anywhere else. Beth-arabah has been met already on the northern boundary, where it was described as a town of this desert afterwards assigned to Benjamin.

The city of Salt gets its name from its neighbourhood. Clarke places it near the lake whose waters are perhaps the saltest in the world, in a country that abounds with salt throughout, and reports the suggestion that it is the same place as Zoar, where Lot escaped after the destruction of Sodom. Keil and Delitzsch put it more precisely at the southern end of the Dead Sea in the Salt Valley, and identify it by what happened there, the Edomites having sustained repeated defeats on that ground in the campaigns of David and of later kings.

Engedi is the one name in the desert list that nobody has to argue about. Clarke translates it as the well of the kid and places it between Jericho and the Dead Sea; Keil and Delitzsch identify it with Ain-Jidi, a spring on a shelf of the high rock above that sea, which the Onomasticon had already called a very large village, and recall that David fled there from Saul. Which is the quiet point of the district: the tract that reads as the least valuable part of Judah's inheritance is the one whose names the books of Samuel would make familiar.
63:
Who the Jebusites were is disputed before anything is said about what happened to them. Gill reports a rabbinic account, which Kimchi passes on and Jarchi accepts, that they were not of the seven nations at all: a Philistine named Jebus, of the seed of Abimelech, gave the place his name, and his descendants who lived there were called after him — which is how Araunah the Jebusite came to be king of it. Gill says the story has no foundation, and that these Jebusites were beyond doubt Canaanites. Calvin met the same fable and read its motive: some Jewish expositors, unwilling to admit their countrymen's sluggishness, invented a covenant with Abraham under which descendants of Abimelech could not lawfully be expelled.

What actually happened is reconstructed differently by each, because the later books do not agree on the surface. Keil and Delitzsch take the notice to look back to the years just after Joshua, when the men of Judah had taken Jerusalem and burnt it but could not hold it, and argue that it contradicts neither later statement, since it says neither that Jerusalem belonged to Judah nor that Judah alone claimed it against Benjamin. Wesley has the city taken in part by Joshua while the upper and stronger portion, Zion, stayed Jebusite until David; from there its holders came down and retook the lower town, so that Israel had to win the place a second and even a third time. Clarke calls the whole history before David encumbered with difficulties, notes that the city is attributed now to Judah and now to Benjamin, and concludes that, lying on the frontier of both, each probably held a part; if the Jebusites were ever expelled before David they recovered at least the stronghold of Zion, which he took from them. Wesley works out the division: the greater part stood in Benjamin, which is why it appears in that tribe's list and not this one, while Moriah, where the temple was built, and Zion once taken belonged to Judah.

The failure itself is what Calvin will not let pass. It furnishes no excuse, and is not set down as one; had they exerted themselves to the full measure of their strength and still failed, the dishonour would have fallen on God, who had promised to remain their leader until they had full possession and to send hornets before them. That they could not do it means only that their own torpor and their neglect of the command, from a love of ease, were the real obstacles. He turns it into a rule: we ought to make vigorous trial of our strength in attempting what God commands, and let no opportunity slip, lest while we are idly resting the door be shut — a moderate delay might have been blameless, but long effeminate ease in a manner refused the blessing God stood ready to give. Wesley reaches the same verdict by another route, laying the failure to unbelief — as Christ could do no mighty work where the people did not believe — and to the sloth by which they forfeited God's help. Ellicott observes that the book records exactly these failures for the three great tribes, Judah here and Ephraim and Manasseh in the chapters following, the full account for all of them being reserved for Judges.

Clarke ends on two cautions about the text rather than the history. The verse dates the book: the Jebusites dwelt with the children of Judah when this was set down, which they did not after David's time, so the writing must precede the kings of Judea. And the catalogue behind it should be read with allowance — names have changed, some are repeated that should have been given once, some confounded with the words describing them; but not every repetition is a copyist's carelessness, since two places often bear one name.
